candidates.statement: Subjects enrolled in clinical trials for the preventive treatment of migraine should have a 59 diagnosis of either chronic migraine or episodic migraine. Chronic migraine is defined by the 60 ICHD as headache occurring on 15 or more days per month for more than 3 months, which, on at 61 least 8 days per month, has the features of migraine headache. Patients with chronic migraine 62 may overuse acute medication and may also fulfill the ICHD criteria for medication overuse 63 headache. 5 Randomization of subjects with chronic migraine into clinical trials should be 64 stratified based on the presence or absence of a concomitant diagnosis of medication overuse 65 headache. Patients with episodic migraine have intermittent, recurrent attacks that meet ICHD 66 criteria 5 for migraine with or without aura, with headache occurring on 14 or fewer days per 67 month. Subjects eligible for enrollment in a chronic or episodic migraine clinical trial should 68 have confirmation of the diagnosis based on their monthly frequency of migraine or headache 69 during a baseline observation period. 70

candidates.statement: Subjects enrolled in clinical trials should have a diagnosis of either chronic migraine or episodic 97 migraine, as stated previously. Migraine subjects with and without aura may be enrolled in 98 confirmatory trials. The time since initial diagnosis of migraine should be at least 12 months 99 before enrollment, with eligibility at enrollment based on a minimum 3-month history of 100 migraine frequency, and with confirmation of migraine frequency observed during a minimum 1- 101 month prospective baseline period (although a longer baseline period can provide a more stable 102 estimate of migraine frequency). Although trials should attempt to enroll a broad age range of 103 subjects, the age at the time of initial migraine diagnosis should generally be younger than 50 104 years old to decrease the chance of enrolling subjects with headaches attributable to another 105 underlying disorder that may mimic migraine (e.g., a brain neoplasm, stroke, temporal arteritis, 106 etc.). If subjects have more than one headache type, they should be able to distinguish their other 107 headache types (e.g., tension-type headaches) from their migraines. 108

candidates.statement: During the conduct of early trials, and until the drug-drug interaction liability of the drug is 136 adequately understood, concomitant medications should be avoided. Assuming no important 137 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic drug-drug interactions are anticipated, sponsors can use 138 concomitant preventive medications for migraine in later stage trials, but only if the dosage of 139 those concomitant medications has been stable for an adequately justified period of time before 140 inclusion into the trial. Subjects should also remain on stable doses of the concomitant drug 141 during the entire duration of the trial. Sponsors should document prior and concomitant use of 142 preventive treatments for migraine during the screening phase of the trials. 143
candidates.context: 4. Concomitant Medications 134 Drugs used for the preventive treatment of migraine are also often used for the treatment of 145 nonmigraine indications and/or can be used to treat other comorbid disorders (e.g., epilepsy, 146 depression, hypertension); therefore, sponsors should clearly document the diagnosis associated 147 with each treatment. Because the use of other preventive migraine treatments may influence the 148 interpretation of both safety and efficacy, no more than 30 percent of the study population should 149 be taking a concomitant medication for the preventive treatment of migraine during the trial, and 150 randomization should be stratified by the use of such concomitant medications. Subjects taking 151 more than one such concomitant preventive medication should typically not be enrolled. 152

candidates.statement: In episodic migraine trials, the primary efficacy endpoint should assess the change from baseline 163 in the number of monthly migraine days (see the migraine day example below). For chronic 164 migraine trials, sponsors may use the change from baseline in the number of monthly migraine 165 days or in the number of monthly headache days (of moderate/severe intensity and/or requiring 166 use of an acute migraine medication) as the primary efficacy endpoint. In the latter scenario, the 167 change from baseline in monthly migraine days should be evaluated as a secondary efficacy 168 endpoint instead. 169

candidates.statement: A patient-reported outcome (PRO) is any report of the status of a patient’s health condition that 216 comes directly from a patient, without interpretation of the patient’s response by a clinician or 217 other person. In clinical studies for migraine, the primary endpoint is typically patient reported. 218 Other PRO instruments can also be used as secondary endpoints to assess treatment benefit. 219 Sponsors that intend to develop and/or include a PRO instrument in their programs should 220 engage early with the review division. In general, instruments should assess concepts or 221 domains that are important to patients, are sensitive to clinically meaningful change, have 222 scoring that can be easily interpreted, and have a recall period that is appropriate for the 223 proposed study design and endpoints. Further information on using a validated PRO may be 224 found in the draft guidances for industry Patient-Focused Drug Development: Selecting, 225 Developing, or Modifying Fit-for-Purpose Clinical Outcome Assessments and Patient-Focused 226 Drug Development: Incorporating Clinical Outcome Assessments Into Endpoints For Regulatory 227 Decision-Making (April 2023). 9

candidates.statement: The primary efficacy analysis should compare the reduction from baseline in monthly migraine 232 days (or headache days) between treatment groups during a prospectively defined evaluation 233 period. The pharmacodynamic and/or pharmacokinetic (PK) characteristics of a drug may 234 inform the appropriate duration of this period. Sponsors may choose to define this evaluation 235 period as the entire double-blind treatment period (i.e., a minimum of 3 months), or alternatively, 236 over the last month of this period. If the primary efficacy analysis only considers the final month 237 of the double-blind treatment period, then a sensitivity analysis should assess the entire post- 238 randomization period. 239
candidates.context: 8. Statistical Considerations 230 To improve the precision of treatment effect estimation and inference, sponsors could consider 241 adjusting for prespecified baseline factors (e.g., baseline use of concomitant medications for 242 preventive treatment of migraine or baseline number of monthly headache/migraine days) that 243 are anticipated to be prognostic of the outcome. If randomization is stratified by baseline 244 covariates, the analysis should account for the stratified randomization. 245

candidates.statement: Phase 1 trials, during which the investigational drug is administered under close medical 256 supervision, provide the best opportunity to obtain safety data at time points close to 257 administration of the investigational drug. At a minimum, these early study safety assessments 258 should include vital signs; laboratory evaluations including hematology, serum chemistry, and 259 urinalysis; and a 12-lead electrocardiogram, at appropriate intervals pre- and post-dose. Vital 260 signs and electrocardiography should be assessed around the expected maximum concentration 261 for the investigational drug and its major metabolites. Sponsors should include risk assessments 262 for QT prolongation. Sponsors should obtain safety data during long-term phase 3 studies at 263 baseline and at appropriate intervals post treatment. The design of clinical studies should take 264 into consideration the results of the nonclinical studies, 10 prior human experience, and any other 265 specific safety concerns with the investigational drug or with other drugs of the same class. 266
candidates.context: B. Safety Considerations 254 New molecular entities should follow the safety recommendations in the ICH guidance for 268 industry E1A The Extent of Population Exposure to Assess Clinical Safety: For Drugs Intended 269 for Long-Term Treatment of Non-Life-Threatening Conditions (March 1995) . The safety 270 experience should be at relevant doses and frequency of administration, including substantial 271 experience at the highest dose and highest frequency of administration proposed for marketing. 272 The submission of additional product-specific safety data may also be necessary, including 273 additional nonclinical studies and/or safety studies in populations at risk either before or post 274 approval. Consultation with FDA is advised early in the development program, especially if a 275 safety signal has already been identified. 276

candidates.statement: Migraine is a relatively common disorder in children. The migraine phenotype is somewhat 291 different between the adult and pediatric populations, and one cannot assume that a drug 292 effective in adults will also be effective in children. Therefore, studies in the pediatric 293 population are needed to determine pediatric efficacy. Of those children diagnosed before 6 years of age, even a smaller proportion of 296 subjects are likely to require preventive therapy; therefore, studies of preventive treatment of 297 either chronic or episodic migraine are considered highly impracticable. For those applications 298 that are subject to section 505B of the FD&C Act (i.e., applications for a new active ingredient, 299 new indication, new dosage form, new dosing regimen, or new route of administration), and thus 300 required to conduct pediatric studies, partial waivers of the pediatric study requirements are 301 appropriate for studies of episodic migraine in subjects younger than 6 years of age. Chronic 302 migraine typically develops after the onset of episodic migraine and thus is rare in children 303 younger than 12 years old. Therefore, for those applications that are subject to section 505B of 304 the FD&C Act, and thus required to conduct pediatric studies, partial waivers are appropriate for 305 studies of chronic migraine in subjects younger than 12 years old.
